profile.purpose: An informal side-by-side test of three ways to crack eggs (on a flat surface, on the edge of a bowl, and egg against egg). It judges each on how easy it is and how many yolks stay intact.
profile.thesis: In this small test, cracking on the flat surface Kenji normally uses was the hardest and broke the most yolks. Cracking on the edge of a bowl was easiest and cleanest, so he decides to switch to it.
key_takeaways: Three methods are tested with six eggs each: flat surface, bowl edge and egg on egg.
The flat-surface method, Kenji's usual one, broke two yolks and was the hardest to crack.
Cracking on the bowl edge was easier and broke fewer yolks.
Egg-on-egg cracking was also easy and fun, like a game of conkers, but it leaves you with one last uncracked egg.
Unwashed farm eggs may carry bacteria such as salmonella on the shell, which cracking can push inside the egg.
Kenji says the sample size is too small to be truly scientific.
Kenji concludes he will switch to cracking eggs on the edge of a bowl.

outline.title: Experimenting with methods
outline.summary: Kenji explains that he has never tested egg-cracking methods. He sets up a test of six eggs each, cracked on a flat surface, on a bowl edge, and egg on egg.

outline.title: Flat surface cracking
outline.summary: He cracks six eggs one-handed on a flat surface, his usual method, and loses two yolks.

outline.title: Bowl edge cracking
outline.summary: He cracks eggs on the edge of a bowl and finds it easier, with fewer broken yolks. He also notes the risk of pushing contamination from the outside of unwashed farm eggs into the egg.

outline.title: Egg on egg cracking
outline.summary: He knocks eggs against each other, compares it to a game of conkers, and watches which egg survives. He is then left with a final egg and nothing to crack it on.

outline.title: Final results and switch
outline.summary: After one more flat-surface test, he sums up the results and decides to switch to cracking on the edge of a bowl.
